pre:
About OneBase

Recovery equipment, and the software that runs it.

OneBase builds commercial hyperbaric, cold, heat and light equipment, and the software on each unit.

We were founded by an engineer, a hyperbaric physician and a designer with a single goal: to make advanced recovery technology accessible, reliable, and beautiful enough for the world’s most demanding wellness environments.

It started with him and hyperbaric oxygen. His way of working, with a plan before, during and after every session, now runs through everything we build.

Our mission

Recovery technology engineered for outcomes.

We believe recovery and longevity technology should be as rigorous in its engineering as it is in its outcomes.

OneBase exists to give commercial operators access to high-quality hyperbaric, contrast therapy, infrared sauna and light therapy equipment, backed by medical expertise, built to last, and designed to elevate any facility.

Our strategy

We build the equipment, and the software that makes it easy to run.

An integrated ecosystem

Hyperbaric, cold, heat and light equipment, the app and the protocols, built to work together. One supplier, one install team and one support contact.

Medically led

Protocols set by Dr. Scott Sherr, so a session is delivered the same way by every member of staff, at every site.

Built for commercial use

Equipment made to run all day in gyms, studios, team facilities, hotels and clinics, with as little as possible for staff to manage.

Software that runs the room

Units are run from a touchscreen on the unit, with schedules that switch saunas and cold rooms on and off by themselves. The OneBase app adds control from a phone and doctor-built protocols.

High quality

We design and manufacture using premium materials, advanced technology, and quality-control standards built for high-frequency commercial use.

Medical expertise

Our medical advisory and leadership team includes practicing hyperbaric specialists who inform product decisions, protocols, and operator education.

Clean design

Recovery technology should enhance a space, not compromise it. Our products are aesthetically considered without sacrificing commercial function.

Precor Wellness, powered by OneBase. OneBase Health’s commercial-grade recovery hardware and OneBase OS software platform, with Precor’s global sales and service network. About the partnership

Dr. Scott Sherr

Co-founder and Chief Medical Officer

Dr. Scott is the physician OneBase was founded around. He is a board certified internal medicine physician, certified in hyperbaric oxygen therapy and Health Optimization Medicine, with more than a decade in hyperbaric practice.

At OneBase he sets the protocols, informs product decisions and leads operator education, so the people running the equipment know how to get the most from it.

It’s not if hyperbaric therapy is going to be helpful, it’s likely when.

His philosophy

The key is integration.

Dr. Scott’s view, from more than a decade of practice, is that a session does more as part of a plan than on its own, and that heat, cold, light and oxygen do more together than apart. He asks one question: what are you doing before, during and after to get the most from it?

It’s when, not if

Timing matters. A session this week and a goal six months away call for different plans, so start with what you are trying to achieve.

Build the foundation

Hyperbaric oxygen works by shifting your physiology, and your body needs the capacity to respond: to make energy and to detoxify. Hydration, minerals and nutrition come first, or alongside.

Before, during and after

Every session has three parts. Prepare before you go in, pair your time in the chamber with something that helps, and use the hours after.

Stack the technologies

Tools combined in the right order go further than any one alone. This comes from his clinical experience; it is hard to isolate in a single study.

Make it personal

There is no one protocol for everybody. The plan follows the person and the goal.

The team

Our leadership.

Andrew Stead

Co-founder and CEO

A mechanical engineer who works directly with the factories that build OneBase equipment. Andrew leads manufacturing, supply and installation, and the growth of OneBase in venues around the world.

Faye Westlund

Co-founder and Chief Design Officer

Faye leads design at OneBase, from the look of the equipment to how the app and a venue’s daily routine fit together. Her focus is making recovery easy for staff to run and something members keep coming back to.

Dan Rozsa

Chief Operating Officer

Dan leads operations, installations and customer success. He came to OneBase from Goldman Sachs and makes sure every install is delivered properly and every customer is looked after once it is running.

Engineering

Technical leadership.

Dr. Simon Benson

Chief Technology Officer

Simon holds a PhD and founded SenseAgent, an industrial sensing platform that was acquired by Philips. He leads engineering at OneBase: the control systems inside the equipment and OneBase OS, the software that runs it.

Whether you run a recovery studio, a gym, a performance centre, a hotel or a clinic, we can help you plan a recovery space that fits your floor and your numbers.

title: Hyperbaric oxygen for clinics · OneBase Health
desc: Clinics already have the medical oversight hyperbaric needs, and it sits alongside the care they already give.
pre:
Hyperbaric in clinics

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy

Delivered under clinical supervision, alongside your treatment plans.

01

What it is

Sitting or lying in a pressurised chamber, usually for 60–90 minutes. Medical-grade chambers deliver oxygen at higher pressure; soft chambers use air at lower pressure.

Quiet and long. In the US it is a prescription medical device, run under medical supervision.

The scienceShow

How it works

Under pressure, more oxygen dissolves directly into the blood plasma (Henry’s law), raising oxygen levels in tissue beyond what red blood cells alone can carry. Medical hyperbaric treatment uses 100% oxygen at about 2–3 atmospheres. Soft chambers run at lower pressure, around 1.3 atmospheres, with air.

Key research

A review of how hyperbaric oxygen raises tissue oxygen and its effects on infection, inflammation and new blood vessel growth.

In diabetic foot ulcers, hyperbaric oxygen improved healing at 6 weeks, but not at long-term follow-up.

Across 10 trials using clinical protocols, hyperbaric oxygen sped recovery from exercise-induced muscle injury but did not reduce soreness overall.

Soft chambers under 1.4 atmospheres are FDA-cleared for acute mountain sickness only, and the Society knows of no reliable evidence of other therapeutic effects at that pressure.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

The established medical uses rely on 100% oxygen at 2–3 atmospheres under medical supervision. Evidence for sports recovery is small and mixed, and there is no reliable evidence for mild pressure with air.

02

How clinics run it

Run by trained staff under clinical direction, with screening before the first session.

title: Sauna for clinics · OneBase Health
desc: Infrared heat is gentler than a traditional sauna, which suits a wider range of patients.
pre:
Sauna in clinics

Infrared heat

A lower air temperature than a traditional sauna, so more patients can use it.

01

What it is

Dry heat you sit in for 15–30 minutes. Infrared runs at 135–149°F; a traditional stone-heater sauna runs hotter.

The most familiar recovery habit. People already know what to do.

The scienceShow

How it works

Heat raises skin and core temperature. Heart rate rises, blood vessels in the skin widen and you sweat, a load on the cardiovascular system similar to moderate exercise. Repeated sessions lead to heat adaptation, including more blood plasma. Infrared cabins warm the body directly at lower air temperatures than a traditional sauna.

Key research

In 2,315 Finnish men followed for about 21 years, sauna 4–7 times a week was associated with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality than once a week.

A review linking regular Finnish sauna with lower blood pressure, less arterial stiffness and better blood-vessel function.

Three weeks of post-training sauna increased runners’ time to exhaustion and plasma volume.

A far-infrared sauna session after endurance training was followed by better jump performance than no sauna.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

The long-term health findings are observational, from Finnish men, and can’t prove cause and effect. Recovery and infrared-specific trials are small and short.

How clinics run it

A gentler infrared cabin, used as directed alongside other care.

title: Cold therapy for clinics · OneBase Health
desc: A dry cold room gives patients cold exposure with no water to manage and no slip risk.
pre:
Cold in clinics

Whole-body cold

Cold therapy without ice baths or wet floors.

01

What it is

Whole-body cold for a few minutes at a time. OneBase’s cold room holds 32–40°F with electric refrigeration, with no water.

Short and intense. Most people build up from a minute or two.

The scienceShow

How it works

Cold narrows blood vessels and lowers tissue temperature, which may limit swelling and dull the sensation of soreness. It also triggers a strong release of noradrenaline, linked to alertness and mood. Water pulls heat away far faster than air, so a dry cold room at 32–40°F is a milder, more tolerable dose than an ice bath or a −100°C cryotherapy chamber.

Key research

Across 17 small trials, cold-water immersion reduced muscle soreness 24–96 hours after exercise compared with passive rest.

Cold-water immersion was slightly better than passive recovery for soreness, best at 11–15°C for 11–15 minutes.

Immersion in 14°C water raised noradrenaline by 530% and dopamine by 250%.

Cold-water immersion straight after every strength session blunted gains in muscle size and strength over 12 weeks.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

The research tests cold water or extreme-cold chambers, not cold air at 32–40°F. It mostly measures how sore people feel. Straight after strength training, regular cold may reduce muscle gains, so timing matters.

02

How clinics run it

Used as directed, with staff nearby. A dry room avoids wet floors in a clinical space.

title: Red light therapy for clinics · OneBase Health
desc: Red light sessions need no hands-on time, so patients can book them around treatment.
pre:
Red light in clinics

Red and near-infrared light

Booked around appointments, with no clinician time needed.

01

What it is

Red and near-infrared light from an LED bed or panel. You lie or stand in front of it for 10–20 minutes.

No heat or cold to put up with, so it’s the easiest one for first-timers.

The scienceShow

How it works

Red (about 630–670 nm) and near-infrared (about 800–950 nm) light is absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase, an enzyme in the mitochondria. The leading theory is that this helps cells make more energy (ATP) and triggers short-lived signals linked to lower inflammation. Dose matters: too little does nothing, and too much can cancel the effect.

Key research

Across 39 trials, light applied to muscles showed some effect on performance and fatigue, with evidence rated very low to moderate quality.

Light applied before exercise modestly increased time to exhaustion and repetitions versus placebo.

In a controlled trial using full-body light units, treated participants had improved skin roughness and collagen density.

A review of whole-body light found possible sleep benefits, but no effect on fatigue markers or exercise performance.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

Most positive performance results come from lasers or LED clusters on specific muscles. Whole-body evidence is thinner and points mainly to skin and possibly sleep.

How clinics run it

Patients book it around their appointments. It needs no hands-on time, so it adds no clinician hours.

01

What it is

Sitting or lying in a pressurised chamber, usually for 60–90 minutes. Medical-grade chambers deliver oxygen at higher pressure; soft chambers use air at lower pressure.

Quiet and long. In the US it is a prescription medical device, run under medical supervision.

The scienceShow

How it works

Under pressure, more oxygen dissolves directly into the blood plasma (Henry’s law), raising oxygen levels in tissue beyond what red blood cells alone can carry. Medical hyperbaric treatment uses 100% oxygen at about 2–3 atmospheres. Soft chambers run at lower pressure, around 1.3 atmospheres, with air.

Key research

A review of how hyperbaric oxygen raises tissue oxygen and its effects on infection, inflammation and new blood vessel growth.

In diabetic foot ulcers, hyperbaric oxygen improved healing at 6 weeks, but not at long-term follow-up.

Across 10 trials using clinical protocols, hyperbaric oxygen sped recovery from exercise-induced muscle injury but did not reduce soreness overall.

Soft chambers under 1.4 atmospheres are FDA-cleared for acute mountain sickness only, and the Society knows of no reliable evidence of other therapeutic effects at that pressure.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

The established medical uses rely on 100% oxygen at 2–3 atmospheres under medical supervision. Evidence for sports recovery is small and mixed, and there is no reliable evidence for mild pressure with air.

What it is

Dry heat you sit in for 15–30 minutes. Infrared runs at 135–149°F; a traditional stone-heater sauna runs hotter.

The scienceShow

How it works

Heat raises skin and core temperature. Heart rate rises, blood vessels in the skin widen and you sweat, a load on the cardiovascular system similar to moderate exercise. Repeated sessions lead to heat adaptation, including more blood plasma. Infrared cabins warm the body directly at lower air temperatures than a traditional sauna.

Key research

In 2,315 Finnish men followed for about 21 years, sauna 4–7 times a week was associated with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality than once a week.

A review linking regular Finnish sauna with lower blood pressure, less arterial stiffness and better blood-vessel function.

Three weeks of post-training sauna increased runners’ time to exhaustion and plasma volume.

A far-infrared sauna session after endurance training was followed by better jump performance than no sauna.

The long-term health findings are observational, from Finnish men, and can’t prove cause and effect. Recovery and infrared-specific trials are small and short.

pre:
Cold in sports teams

Post-game cold

The squad cools down together. No ice to buy, no tubs to drain.

01

What it is

Whole-body cold for a few minutes at a time. OneBase’s cold room holds 32–40°F with electric refrigeration, with no water.

Short and intense. Most people build up from a minute or two.

The scienceShow

How it works

Cold narrows blood vessels and lowers tissue temperature, which may limit swelling and dull the sensation of soreness. It also triggers a strong release of noradrenaline, linked to alertness and mood. Water pulls heat away far faster than air, so a dry cold room at 32–40°F is a milder, more tolerable dose than an ice bath or a −100°C cryotherapy chamber.

Key research

Across 17 small trials, cold-water immersion reduced muscle soreness 24–96 hours after exercise compared with passive rest.

Cold-water immersion was slightly better than passive recovery for soreness, best at 11–15°C for 11–15 minutes.

Immersion in 14°C water raised noradrenaline by 530% and dopamine by 250%.

Cold-water immersion straight after every strength session blunted gains in muscle size and strength over 12 weeks.

What the evidence doesn’t show yet

The research tests cold water or extreme-cold chambers, not cold air at 32–40°F. It mostly measures how sore people feel. Straight after strength training, regular cold may reduce muscle gains, so timing matters.

What is the IceVault?

A self-contained, dry cold-immersion room that uses electric refrigeration to hold 34–40°F, delivering the benefits of cold exposure without water, ice or nitrogen.

How is it different from a cold plunge or cryotherapy chamber?

No water or ice. No setup, cleanup or wet floors. Longer sessions (3–15 minutes) at tolerable temperatures. Multiple users at once. Less maintenance.

Is it safe?

Yes. It removes the gas-exposure risk of cryotherapy and the slippery wet floors of ice baths. Breathable air and controlled temperatures keep the experience comfortable.

Does it need special installation?

No. The IceVault is plug-and-play: a power connection, no plumbing or drainage.

Depending on configuration, 1–8 users simultaneously.

An automated self-cleaning system keeps the environment sanitary with minimal effort. OneBase support helps with troubleshooting.

Ketones are products of dietary fat breakdown which can also be taken as supplements. They are readily used by our mitochondria, the batteries of our cells, to make energy.

In addition, ketones protect the body from the mild stress of increased oxygen in circulation during hyperbaric therapy. It’s a good thing you are in a hyperbaric chamber because now you have an ample supply of oxygen to meet the demands of the target tissue. In addition, the pressure inside the chamber will pump out cellular debris, moving it into your body’s lymphatic or garbage collection system.

Hydration

Hydration is key before, during, and after your Optimal Focus Protocol. Drink mineral-infused water, use mineral sachets (added to your water), or even add a pinch of sea salt to your water if that’s all you have available.

Why minerals?

When there are minerals in the water (sodium, calcium, selenium, potassium, boron, magnesium, and others), the water you drink will be absorbed more efficiently keeping you better hydrated. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy works by infusing oxygen directly into the blood plasma (liquid of our blood). If you are dehydrated, there will be less blood plasma and correspondingly, less oxygen infused and taken to where it’s needed. In addition, minerals are essential to energy (ATP) production at the cellular level. During HBOT, we are increasing ATP production because of the increased oxygen in circulation. As a result, your body’s requirement for minerals will also increase.

During

Pair your HBOT session with 4-7-8 breathing to reach calm, relaxed control.

Breathing technique

Optimal Focus requires calm, relaxed control. When we are stressed, our sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight) is activated and this negatively affects focus and performance. The key is to increase parasympathetic (rest, calm, and digest) activation and one of the fastest and most efficient ways to do this is by using various breathing techniques that prolong exhalation.

While in the chamber, we suggest you try the 4-7-8 breathing technique. In 4-7-8, you inhale to the count of 4, hold your breath for a count of 7, and then slowly exhale for a count of 8. The goal is to do this 5 to 10 times in succession but even after just one or two rounds, you’ll likely feel more calm and relaxed. If 4-7-8 relaxes you to the point of napping, that’s perfect. This is called an “oxygen nap” and it will be one of the most rejuvenating naps you’ve ever experienced.

Cold improves blood flow and detox, wakes you up, boosts your focus and leaves you feeling blissful.

Cold therapy

Cold Therapy after your Optimal Focus protocol serves two major purposes. The first is cold therapy increases blood and lymphatic flow. When under actual cold conditions, the body constricts blood peripheral vessels and diverts blood to the most essential organs (brain, heart, lungs) to keep them alive and warm. When the cold is removed, there is a rapid warming and dilation of blood vessels, including those in your periphery (skin, scalp, feet, etc) with blood and lymphatic flow rushing there.

The second purpose of cold therapy post HBOT is due to the release of neurotransmitters associated with focus such as norepinephrine and epinephrine, endocannabinoids (our body’s natural cannabinoids) like Anandamide which is known as the “bliss molecule”, and endorphins which make us feel good as well.

Choices for cold therapy include cold water immersion (tubs, rivers, lakes), cryotherapy in a cryotherapy chamber, or even a cold shower. Typical cold exposure is from 2 to 5 minutes depending on type and temperature of the cold therapy.

Before

Hydration improves both blood and lymphatic flow, which is needed to bounce back faster. For an extra kick, increasing your glutathione levels helps to optimize detox.

Mineral hydration

Most of us are chronically dehydrated (especially when we are stressed) and mineral-infused water is the fastest way to hydrate. When you drink mineral-infused water, a hydration sachet, or even get to your local IV bar to hydrate, this water bathes your blood vessels and improves both blood and lymphatic flow. And the minerals bathe your cells, giving them the cofactors they need to make energy more effectively.

Multivitamins

Those of us who are chronically stressed are also very likely nutrient deficient as well due to a poor diet or poor absorption of nutrients (vitamins, minerals, antioxidants) from our diet. The best way to improve your nutrient levels quickly is by taking a comprehensive multivitamin. This multivitamin should contain activated or methylated B-vitamins because they are more easily absorbed and utilized by the body. Make sure it also contains the major antioxidants like Vitamin C, D, K2, E, A, and Glutathione (or NAC)! Take it 30 minutes to an hour prior to HBOT.

Glutathione

Glutathione is your master antioxidant. It is often depleted when the body/brain is under stress and there is acute and especially prolonged inflammation. Repleting glutathione levels is essential to optimizing detox and resilience to stress.

During

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy works on reducing the inflammation. Since your body is working hard it’s important for you to rest.

Meditation or relaxation

The key to recovering from a viral illness is to take time to rest and become more parasympathetic. And the good news is that inside a hyperbaric chamber, you are isolated from the outside world for just a little bit to make this easier. It is best to turn your phone onto airplane mode or off and instead, focus on meditation or relaxation techniques. For meditation, consider a focused practice like focusing on your breath or object. For relaxation techniques, consider progressive muscle relaxation where you tense a muscle and then let it go every 15 to 30 seconds.

After

Vibration boosts the lymphatic system, and an infrared sauna increases blood circulation and helps you sweat out the toxins.

Vibration

Whole body vibration stimulates your body’s lymphatic system to work more efficiently in removing waste and detoxifying. After HBOT, this is a great way to supercharge recovery. 5 to 10 minutes is all you need. The sooner the better after HBOT.

Infrared sauna

Infrared saunas use infrared light to heat your body up from the inside out, increasing blood circulation and revving up your detox pathways while you sweat out toxins. The key to recovering from a viral illness is to focus on detox post HBOT. One of the best ways to do this is to head into your infrared sauna for 15 to 45 minutes and sweat it out (while keeping hydrated!) after HBOT.

If you are very weak, even start with 5 to 10 minutes first. The infrared heat will increase blood flow and lymphatic throughout the body. After you leave the sauna, take a lukewarm shower and hydrate some more.

As with all HBOT related protocols, mineral hydration is key. When you are bouncing back from a viral illness, it is essential you do this after HBOT as well as before.
